#4264. Yakuza Creator Toshiro Nagoshi's Studio Has Officially Shut Down, Ending Gang Of Dragon's Development With It

Nagoshi Studio, the developer led by Yakuza/Like a Dragon series creator Toshiro Nagoshi, has officially shut down, ending development of Gang of Dragon, which was revealed at The Game Awards last year. Shareholders resolved to dissolve the studio on October 31, according to a notice published in a Japanese government newspaper called Kanpo, as first reported by Gematsu.

This follows a report from Bloomberg earlier this year that said Chinese gaming megacorp NetEase Games was cutting funding to Nagoshi Studio, allowing Nagoshi to seek independent funding elsewhere. It seems he couldn't find funding, and now Nagoshi Studio is no more. NetEase helped Nagoshi found the studio in November 2021.

You can watch the Gang of Dragon reveal trailer below for a look at what the team was cooking up:

This closure follows other signals that NetEase is looking to divest from the gaming scene outside of its Chinese studios. A little over a month ago, Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture left NetEase to go independent again, just months after the launch of Romeo Is A Dead Man.

#4263. The Wrapp - Warhammer Survivors, chickens crossing colourful roads, and feline Sudoku

Hello! And welcome back to The Wrapp. This time, a bunch of the team have been swept up in Warhammer fever, though they disagree on its quality. Elsewhere, Dann is ticking along with his usual smorgasbord of games while Shaun is losing sleep counting cats. Apparently, they're less therapeutic than sheep. I assume because they look less like fluffy clouds.

Warhammer Survivors… Need I say more? Okay, I'll say a bit more. Leading up to its release, Warhammer Survivors touted that it was going to be just that: Vampire Survivors with Warhammer theming, visuals, and a couple of tweaked mechanics. And it has succeeded very well. It is perhaps one of the greatest waiting games released since Angry Birds, and I'm looking forward to exploring more of it and any DLC that comes with it.

And to those certain reviews that have criticised it for not blowing their minds… What were you expecting? We were all told that we were gonna get a duck and we got a duck. If you downloaded and played expecting a goose, my friend, that's on you.

Unfortunately, I have succumbed to peer pressure (and by that, I mean Will and Iwan) and have downloaded Warhammer Survivors on my phone. I lasted a full minute before I inevitably died on my first go. I wish I could say that a fearsome boss took me down in a blaze of glory after my valiant efforts of trying to overcome it, but in reality, a swarm of rats rushed towards me, I got caught in the stampede, and I promptly perished.

So I guess that means I need to spend the entirety of my weekend trying to take vengeance on those rats. Look out, rodents, here I come!

This week is Into the Wild for Pokémon Go, and so I’ll be spending a large portion of my weekend walking around with fellow trainers, trying to nab shinies and hundos. Outside of that, I’m continuing my search for the perfect run in 80 Days (my most recent run ended with me freezing to death near the North Pole) and keeping chipping away at MH: Outlanders.

I’ll be honest, after playing so much mobile this week, I may be taking a break. I’ve put a lot of time into Warhammer Survivors and, while I’ve been enjoying it, it hasn’t quite clicked with me the way that Vampire Survivors did. Read my whole Warhammer Survivors review for the breakdown, but as many people have opined, it feels a bit like what it is: a simple spinoff that lacks the meat of the original.

That being said, I will be putting more time into it since I’m in a bit of a Warhammer mood. However, Titanium Court is still begging for my attention too. Either way, I’ll be sure to try and put a bit of time into something over the weekend since, well, it’s my job after all. And lord knows I can’t wait to get my hands on Gotrek in Warhammer Survivors!

Being as I am a man of increasing age, my days of gaming until the small hours are behind me, or so I thought. It was but Wednesday night, however, when I found myself accidentally up until 1 am, so enthralled was I by this latest game I found. Was it Ocarina of Time, was it a Grand Theft Auto? No, it was Mewodoku.

For those not in the meknow - see, I can do it too, just not as well - it is the age-old game of Sudoku with cat faces. That's a very reductive description, cause theres also one cat per colour with lines going all over the place. Whatever it is, I am smitten. The puzzles get genuinely challenging, the music is so calming, and I am currently at the top of the leaderboard! It is probably all bots or children, but I will happily stand on top of little Timmy at the summit of Meowdoku.

As you'll know from reading this Wrapp, one game has taken our virtual office by storm. Slaying hordes of enemies in Warhammer Survivors seems to be the order of the day. As such, I've got no choice but to try Crossy Road Rush. That's right. With all the grittiness and gore flying about right now, I fancy a palate cleanser. So I'll dive into the colourful world of endless running for an hour or two. Once its sugary goodness makes me feel a little sick, maybe then I'll pivot to chunky pixel violence.

#4262. Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

Vince Zampella, co-creator of Call of Duty, and a veteran studio head responsible for some of the biggest franchises in the world, is gone.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”

#4261. 10 Great Games That Defined The Original Xbox

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

25 years ago, on November 15th, 2001, the gaming industry was forever changed when Microsoft officially dived into the console gaming market with the debut of its first home console, simply called the Xbox.

Designed to be a bridge between the hardware and software capabilities of PCs and the accessibility of home gaming consoles, the original Xbox console took the world by storm with its revolutionary gaming titles and services, proving that the United States can still rival Japanese gaming prospects.

With the original Xbox, and the overall Xbox brand, celebrating its momentous 25th anniversary this November, here’s a look back at 10 great exclusive games that defined the original Xbox and helped pave the way for Microsoft to become a modern gaming juggernaut.

Today, Xbox is largely known for three exclusive franchises: Halo, Gears of War, and Forza but long before the latter simulation racing series took the Xbox brand by storm during the Xbox 360 era, there was another series that stood as Xbox’s premier exclusive racing franchise: Project Gotham Racing.

Originally released as one of the Xbox’s many launch titles, the first Project Gotham Racing allowed up to four players in split-screen multiplayer to race against each other using 29 of the hottest cars of the early 21st century across San Francisco, London, Tokyo, and New York City.

With its stunt-focused Kudos point system and fun, arcade-like modes, Project Gotham Racing became one of the earliest Platinum Hits on the Xbox, leading to the development of three direct sequels, a few spinoffs, and the hit Xbox Live Arcade game, Geometry Wars.

Every great console needs its own standout amusing party game, and while Nintendo had Mario Party and PlayStation had Crash Bash, Xbox got its own distinct party game in the form of Fuzion Frenzy.

Another Xbox launch title, Fuzion Frenzy was an original party game not based on any prior IP, with the game being set in a futuristic tournament pitting four players against one another across randomized or pre-selected minigames with the goal of obtaining as many orbs and points as possible.

Chaotic minigames like Paint Panic and Falling Star quickly made Fuzion Frenzy a fan-favorite, and while it only got one sequel on the Xbox 360, many players still go back to play its wacky games to this very day (thanks to FF being backwards compatible on every future Xbox platform).

The sixth generation of consoles was a time for beginnings and a time for endings for many in the gaming industry at the time, most notably Sega. The Sega Dreamcast would mark the end for its home console prospects.

However, the failure of the Dreamcast didn’t mark the end for several Sega properties, as Microsoft collaborated with Sega to make the Xbox the exclusive home for several Dreamcast ports and sequels. Arguably the best was the funky Jet Set Radio Future.

A sequel to Jet Grind Radio, Jet Set Radio Future is a hyper stylized action game set in a futuristic Tokyo, where a group of teenagers called the GGs skate throughout the city and spray paint graffiti as a form of resistance against the dominating Rokkaku Group megacorporation.

Fans of the original Xbox who want play adventure titles that feature villains as protagonists should check out these 10 games

The RPG giant that is Bethesda is currently owned by Microsoft, and is a major part of Xbox’s future game investments. The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel is rumored to become a Project Helix exclusive, but long before Microsoft purchased Bethesda, the two companies first collaborated to release The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind exclusively on the original Xbox.

The first Elder Scrolls title to debut on a home console, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind was a first and third-person RPG set in the titular ash-clouded Tamriel province of Morrowind, following a customizable prisoner who sets out on a journey to defeat the oppressive Dagoth Ur.

While Morrowind hasn’t aged as well as its successors, it paved the way for Bethesda to debut other landmark RPGs, such as Fallout, Skyrim, and Starfield on consoles, helping showcase the immense potential of western RPGs.

One of the greatest innovations the original Xbox featured was the creation of Xbox Live, as it was one of the first online multiplayer gaming services designed for home consoles and practically laid the groundwork for all modern online gaming services. Xbox Live’s debut title was MechAssault.

Set in the multimedia BattleTech franchise, MechAssault is a third-person mech shooter game set on the planet Helios. It follows a Wolf's Dragoons BattleMech pilot as they attempt to liberate the planet from the technology-worshipping faction Word of Blake.

MechAssault’s campaign is a lot of fun, but the game is far more famous for its multiplayer as it was one of the first console titles to feature Quick Matches, the ability to host and invite friends to online games, and multiplayer DLC such as new maps, gametypes, and new types of mechs like Raven and Loki.

Every sixth generation console featured fantastic titles that were beloved by many but just didn’t sell well enough to receive proper sequels, resulting in these types of games becoming cult classics. There’s no better Xbox cult classic out there than Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge.

Loosely based on the 1998 Crimson Skies board game, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge has players embody Fortune Hunters air pirate gang leader Nathan Zachary, in an alternate 20th century where planes and zeppelins became the primary mode of transportation and the U.S. split into warring nations.

With an interesting world and story highly reminiscent of classic pulp books and films like Indiana Jones and enthralling third-person fighter plane gameplay, Revenge quickly became a fan-favorite. While it never received a sequel, it has since become the unofficial mascot for Xbox’s backwards compatibility.

These classic games will require some work to play again unless you have an older-gen console.

Early on in the Xbox brand’s history, Xbox’s most famous exclusive franchises were Halo, Gears of War, and Peter Molyneux's highly ambitious fantasy RPG Fable, which is finally set to return to Xbox early next year with a reboot of the series.

The original Fable was claimed by Molyneux to be the most ambitious RPG of the sixth console generation, with the game supposedly allowing players to have children in-game, play through the protagonist’s entire life, and witness plant life grow throughout the game, among other promises.

While most of these features weren’t present in the first Fable game, the original Fable still turned out to be an incredibly charming, comedic, and overall fun RPG, thanks to its witty British humor, morality system, and vast numbers of ways to interact with NPCs such as getting married and farting on people.

Nintendo fans recently got to take part in the midnight launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launch at various gaming stores. Those launch events paled in comparison to the cultural phenomenon that was the launch of Halo 2.

The original Xbox was arguably the house Halo: Combat Evolved built, and as such, most gamers in the world were excited to see how Bungie would improve upon the series in Halo 2, leading to the sequel receiving 1.5 million U.S. pre-orders and selling over 2.4 million copies in its launch day alone.

This anticipation was warranted though, as Halo 2 became the most popular Xbox Live game up until the release of Gears of War 1 and is widely regarded to feature one of the best FPS campaigns of all time thanks to the introduction of the Arbiter, dual-wielding, vehicle hijacking, and more.

The original Xbox was home to very few JRPGs, but these obscure ones might have something left exploring if you're interested.

While Fable 1 is the RPG most associated with the original Xbox, I would argue that it wasn’t the best RPG available on the console, with that honor instead going to BioWare’s epic 2003 masterpiece Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

Many Star Wars video games were released exclusively for the original Xbox, but KOTOR was by far the most notable. It not only took place roughly 4,000 years before the events of the films during the Jedi Civil War, but featured one of the greatest gaming twists of all time, centered around Darth Revan.

KOTOR’s rather clunky round-based combat hasn't exactly aged well over the years, but its story and characters are still regarded as being some of the best to appear any RPG, such as Darth Malak, Jedi Knight Bastila Shan, the murderous droid HK-47, and the Mandalorian Canderous Ordo to name a few.

Finally, without a doubt, the number one exclusive video game that defined the original Xbox and arguably the Xbox brand overall was the launch title and Bungie’s revolutionary FPS Halo: Combat Evolved.

Halo: Combat Evolved was the definitive console-based FPS that truly showcased the capability of consoles to deliver an engaging, fun, and wondrous FPS experience, thanks to its cinematic quality, wide-open spaces, addictive gunplay and vehicle combat, and engrossing FPS multiplayer maps.

If Halo: Combat Evolved hadn’t been packaged with most Xbox consoles on day one, Xbox likely wouldn’t have lasted beyond the sixth generation of consoles and CE’s success ultimately led to Xbox not only obtaining a mascot with Master Chief but the creation of one of the most beloved sci-fi multimedia franchises of all time.

To celebrate Gears of War: E-Day's release and Gears' upcoming 20th anniversary, here's a ranking of every campaign in the Gears of War franchise.

#4260. Love and Deepspace 5.0 update brings together all five love interests for the first time

Love and Deepspace is getting a big update to celebrate its second anniversary, and there's a lot to dig through.

If you can believe it, Love and Deepspace is almost two-years-old, and Infold Games is celebrating the moment in a few major ways. The Throne of Eros update brings the game up to version 5.0, and it’s one for fans of all love interests.

For one, this is the first time all five of them are brought together. The update is also adding some important new features, alongside anniversary events, and more.

Throne of Eros also doubles as the new Wish Pool, which is the one that has all of the game’s love interests in a single banner. This is a limited-time affair, of course, but it’s not the only thing you should look forward to here.

There’s also the Memory Growth Bonus, another limited-time event that you can take advantage of to grow your Memories. The even bigger news is that you can target your Wishes through the Xspace Echo, which lets you select five Memories to create your own pool from. You can use this to get any Memories you might not have, of course.

On the topic of Memories, you’ll also be able to unlock new second anniversary KV Memories, as part of a Yearly Highlights Event that will let you look back on your own journey with the game over the past year.

On the story and narrative side, Throne of Eros adds two new main stories, with new branches for Xavier, and Rafayel. There’s even a narrative-specific event that will run throughout the anniversary period, through which you can earn two daily outfits for each of the five love interests.

The celebrations also extend to new anniversary content like mail, and video calls. You can purchase a Yearly Pass, and check out some new arrivals at the Lunar Shop.

Beyond the anniversary content, version 5.0 also adds a new feature to the game: Home, which essentially offers a hub to get you directly to interacting with love interests that doesn’t have to do with combat or story.

You can also expect various other quality of life updates that touch on the Journal, Phone Moments Search, Resources Quick Cleanup, and new Tete-a-Tete that should make interacting with all of them more streamlined.

While this is a special banner, you should brush up on how banners work in Love and Deepspace if you’re unfamiliar. As always, it’s never not a good idea to check our Love and Deepspace codes page for some freebies.

#4259. Warhammer Survivors reveals its roadmap, with new characters, weapons and cross-save on the way

One of my colleagues gave Warhammer Survivors a go this week and lasted about a minute before a stampede of rats ran them over. The weekend has since been set aside for revenge. Good timing, because Auroch Digital has just revealed a roadmap for the Survivors-like, which is out now on iOS and Android, and there’s a lot more on the way to die to.

Most of the roadmap includes free updates over the next few months, adding new characters and weapons to both the Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar halves, along with QoL fixes. Smaller patches will fill the gaps between the bigger drops, with some of them landing before the end of the year.

Cross-save is coming as well, and since it launched on just about everything at once (phones, Switch, PlayStation, Xbox and PC), being able to carry a run’s worth of unlocks from the sofa to the tube is the update I’d look forward to most. The bigger piece of content is still under wraps, listed only as [REDACTED], with a few clues tucked into the roadmap image for anyone who fancies some detective work.

Our Warhammer Survivors review is live now too, and Iwan’s verdict is that it’s got the heart, but not the spark. The office hasn’t agreed on it either, as this week’s Wrapp makes fairly clear. The thing is, Vampire Survivors didn’t arrive fully formed.

A lot of what people love about it came in over years of updates and expansions, and the version on your phone now is a very different beast from the one that first went viral. Heart’s the harder thing to patch in. If Auroch keeps this pace, I’d back the spark to show up sooner rather than later.

Warhammer Survivors is out now on the App Store and Google Play.

And if the rats keep winning, our list of this week’s new mobile games is somewhere else to spend the weekend.

#4258. Cosy Train Sim 'Station To Station' Arrives On Switch 2 Later This Month

Do you like trains? Of course you do, who doesn't like trains. Stupid question. Anyway, you're in luck, dear reader. The cosy train sim Station to Station is making its way to the Switch 2, launching on 26th November 2026.

Boasting lovely voxel visuals, Station to Station starts you off with a handful of rural structures, tasking you with creating stations and connections to expand your world and transform it into a lush, thriving landscape.

While it's ultimately a relaxing experience, you can also earn high scores by engaging with more strategic gameplay, allowing you to stack bonuses and multiply your income.

On Switch 2, you can expect to find mouse controls along with the game's Creative Mode, letting you explore community designs and share your own. The main game will contain 54 levels set across 7 regions.

Over on Steam, Station to Station currently commands a total of 1,248 user reviews, of which 89% are positive. It's also earned solid scores from critics too, including 8/10 from IGN and 4/5 from Tech Radar.

#4257. Genshin Impact Version Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, including the long-awaited Moon Maiden Columbina

The first major Genshin Impact update in 2026 is almost here, bringing characters we've been waiting a while to play, and more besides.

Genshin Impact’s latest Special Program has spilled all the beans on the game’s next major update, Luna 4. The update, which arrives on January 14, kicks off 2026 with several bits of new content, including some previously-teased characters.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first new arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

Luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

The first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a new outfit in the shop at a discount.

Version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

All around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

All players will receive 1,600 Primogems through the in-game mail. If you log in regularly, you can earn up to ten Intertwined Fates. Lantern Rite has a new outfit for Yaoyao, which is also where you have a chance to earn one 4-Star Liyue character for free.

Finally, you can look forward to the new Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.

#4255. 8 JRPGs With the Most Nominations at The Game Awards

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

The gaming industry is no stranger to award shows. Nowadays, we have countless ceremonies, such as the Golden Joystick Awards, the BAFTA Games Awards, the D.I.C.E. Awards, and more. However, it is hard to deny the massive influence of Geoff Keighley's The Game Awards, whether because of its sheer audience reach, the spectacle, the world-premiere announcements, or the acceptance speeches that become industry touchstones for years to come.

From Nioh to Black Myth: Wukong, these are the seven Soulslikes with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

We're nearing The Game Awards season, so I put together a themed list to celebrate. Rather than just discussing the ceremony itself, why not look back at the JRPGs with the most nominations at The Game Awards? True to my personal branding around here, I went ahead and did just that. It is wild to think that in the past, JRPGs would barely even be considered for major awards, yet here we are. Not only do they regularly rack up nominations today, but a certain JRPG-inspired title even swept the TGAs and currently stands as the most awarded game in the event's history.

Octopath Traveler caught plenty of people by surprise, myself included. Just when we thought Square Enix had left pixel art behind for good, the company proved there is still plenty of room for the visual style while elevating it to new heights with its HD-2D graphical engine. Beyond the visuals, it recaptured the nostalgia of classic Square titles through the core gameplay loop as well.

Octopath Traveler drew heavy inspiration from Final Fantasy VI to weave together the tales of its eight protagonists. That achievement earned the JRPG three nominations: Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, and Best Role Playing Game, all of which felt entirely fitting. It didn't walk away with a trophy, but earning those nods showed how deeply critics appreciated the experience at the time.

It's not every day a JRPG competes for Game of the Year, so when it does, you know the game is an absolute banger. As far as I am concerned, if Xenoblade Chronicles 3 had taken home the top prize, it would have been completely deserved. To be fair, it lost both Best Role-Playing Game and Game of the Year to Elden Ring, which is entirely understandable, even if I would still hand the trophy to Monolith Soft if we were running Murillo's TGAs.

Losing Best Score to God of War Ragnarök, however? Look, I know Ragnarök features a wonderful composition, but anyone who has played Xenoblade Chronicles 3, or any Xenoblade title for that matter, heck, any modern JRPG, knows that musical composition is the beating heart of the genre. You could play a JRPG where every other element falls flat, and I guarantee the soundtrack would still blow you away. But I digress, and that is just the fanboy in me talking. I am simply thrilled that a JRPG received that much recognition and spotlight back in 2022.

Speaking of Best Score, NieR: Automata nailed that category in the year it competed, and honestly, that was the bare minimum. If they hadn't given the score award to Automata, who else could possibly have taken it? I do know who beat it out for Best Role-Playing Game that year, though, and I will get to that entry soon. NieR: Automata also earned a nomination for Best Narrative, and while it didn't win, I can understand why.

The story was insanely good, touching on deep philosophical and existentialist themes that leave you chewing on their meanings for months. However, its narrative delivery and structure can feel a bit complex for some players. You have to play through the game multiple times to get the full picture, and while I had a blast on every playthrough, some folks might drop off after the first ending and miss everything NieR: Automata truly offers. Plus, I haven't played What Remains of Edith Finch, and since the TGAs are ultimately a competition, it may have offered a tighter narrative experience.

Even before Final Fantasy XVI hit store shelves, it was already sparking heated debate. I have never minded the franchise evolving its formula, though certain corners of the fanbase got irked just hearing that Final Fantasy XVI would lean into full action combat. Regardless of the broader discourse, I loved the game. It moved 3 million copies at launch (even if Square Enix wasn't fully satisfied with the numbers) and walked away with 4 nominations at the 2023 TGAs.

Had Final Fantasy XVI not launched in the exact same year as Baldur's Gate 3, it might easily have swept more categories, including Best Role-Playing Game and Best Performance, because let's face it, Ben Starr as Clive was perfection. The JRPG did take home Best Score and Music with Masayoshi Soken at the helm, a victory that was overwhelmingly deserved. To this day, I still blast either the Phoenix or Bahamut theme at the gym and feel like a Dominant hoisting weights.

From Axiom Verge to Hollow Knight: Silksong, these are the ten Metroidvanias with the most nominations at The Game Awards.

Remember how I mentioned that NieR: Automata lost Best Role-Playing Game and that the outcome was pretty justifiable? Well, it lost to Persona 5, and given that it stands as one of my all-time favorite JRPGs and the best-selling Persona entry ever, I completely understand the decision. Furthermore, in TGA history, Persona 5 was the first JRPG to compete for the main Game of the Year prize. It didn't win because it went up against The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and really, who can complain about that outcome?

It still secured Best Role Playing Game over NieR: Automata, Divinity: Original Sin II, and Final Fantasy XV, which speaks to what a stacked year 2017 was for RPG fans. If the votes were up to me, Persona 5 would have swept practically every category and called it a night. It is a JRPG through and through, featuring a slow burn, extensive social sim segments, and mountains of dialogue, yet it still shattered niche barriers to reach a massive global audience. May Atlus keep on winning.

Apparently my wishes were granted in record time, because Atlus kept on winning. While Persona 5 earned 4 nominations, Metaphor: ReFantazio racked up 6 nominations and took home 3 major trophies: Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, and Best Role-Playing Game, edging out Square Enix's own Final Fantasy VII Rebirth. That is an extraordinary feat, mind you. Despite Persona's massive growth, Final Fantasy remains a far more recognizable mainstream brand, making it all the more impressive that critics favored Metaphor.

I adore Metaphor, by the way. It was the very first JRPG I covered right after joining the team here at DualShockers, and I fell in love with it immediately. It is stylish, gutting, gripping, challenging, and endlessly engaging. It came dangerously close to dethroning Persona 5 as my favorite Atlus JRPG, falling just a hair short, though not quite yet. I don't know whether Studio Zero plans to release DLC or jump straight into a follow-up, but I will definitely be there on day one and hope to see its successor pull in even more nominations.

Eagle-eyed readers might notice that I left Final Fantasy VII Remake off this list. That entry received 6 nominations, though including it felt slightly redundant since both games competed in nearly the same categories, simply swapping Best Art Direction for Best Audio Design, while Final Fantasy VII Rebirth added a Best Performance for Briana White as Aerith. She ultimately lost to Melina Juergens as Senua, which is tough luck.

Even so, if we look specifically at Japanese-developed JRPGs (as awkward as that phrasing sounds), Final Fantasy VII Rebirth holds the record for the most nominations in TGA history so far. The title earned nods for Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Score and Music (which it won), Best Audio Design, Best Performance, Best Role-Playing Game (losing to Metaphor: ReFantazio), and Game of the Year (losing to Astro Bot). No matter how hard certain corners of the internet try to downplay Rebirth's success, critics worldwide universally acclaimed it, and I cannot wait to see Final Fantasy VII Revelation rack up just as many nominations and plenty of wins.

We are well past debating whether Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 counts as a JRPG, so I will skip the preamble. What I want to highlight here is something everyone who follows the TGAs already knows: Expedition 33 holds the record as the most awarded game in TGA history. That milestone is not only deeply symbolic for the current climate of the gaming industry, where publishers constantly chase infinite exponential profits, but it also proves that simply throwing massive budgets at a project is not the secret to making a great game.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 represents a union of passionate fans, sheer willpower, rich inspiration, and genuine love for art and video games distilled into something tangible, fun, emotional, and lasting. From the very moment I started playing, I could not put the controller down, completely enthralled by the journey of my Expeditioners. As proof of that obsession, I actually earned the world's first platinum trophy for the game, and I am not kidding. Even director Guillaume Broche himself confirmed it to me on LinkedIn. Not trying to gloat, just showing how transcendental my love for this title truly is.

We're not just talking about Grand Theft Auto VI and Ocarina of Time, but up to seven video games that could sweep The Game Awards.

#4254. Heartopia captures the hearts of Animal Crossing and The Sims fans to become the No.1 free download across 50 countries

Heartopia is officially the first big mobile launch of 2026, as the game grabs the attention of millions worldwide.

Heartopia, the new cosy life sim from XD Games, has officially arrived on mobile, right on schedule. If you’ve been keeping up with Heartopia news, you’re likely already aware that the game has pushed back its Steam release to an indeterminate point in 2026.

Doesn’t look like it mattered much, however, as this has already been a big launch on iOS and Android — it probably helps that PC players aren't being entirely left out of the fun, since the game is already available there via XD's own cross-device platform TapTap.

XD Games announced today that Heartopia has reached the top spot on the App Store’s downloads page for free games, and it managed to do so in more than 50 countries and regions worldwide.

The developer is celebratig by offering players a lot of free stuff. If you're feeling lucky, you’ll find new outfits and furniture in three gacha banners (Gilded Acorn Exhibitions): Polar Hymn, The Frostguard, and Coolplayism.

XD Games says you can expect regular updates to add more content, through Fashionwaves and Festivals. In fact, the first season - Winter Frost - is already penciled in for sometime in late January, and it’s going to add appropriately wintery activities like ice skating and snowman-building.

In February, a My Little Pony collaboration event will kick off, bringing new inspired outfits, and vehicles to the game.

Heartopia is a clever mix of Animal Crossing, and The Sims. It’s a free-to-play life sim where you can create your own character, dress them up, build a home for them (and decorate it), and go about town visiting and playing with other players’ characters.

The game’s main feature is the ability to take on a hobby, and seven of those are available at launch. You can dig deep into each hobby, either alone or with others, and there’s a progression track dedicated to each one.

Whether you’re among the millions who downloaded the game already, or you intend to so soon, we’ve got a set of helpful guides to get you started. You should check out how to unlock and upgrade hobbies in Heartopia first, before you get deep into finding all cooking recipes. And, of course, this wouldn’t be a big game launch without a bunch of Heartopia codes for some free stuff.

#4253. The Elder Scrolls VI Has An Official Subtitle And It's 'Sentinel'

The headline tells the story: The Elder Scrolls VI has an official subtitle and it's Sentinel. So the full game is now titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, or, as we will undoubtedly refer to it moving forward, as we colloquially do with the previous three games (Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim), Sentinel.

The news comes from Bethesda's various social media accounts, which are all sharing the video above. Along with the video, music, and the title, it also shares the text as a quote attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest to High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell (4E 206): "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

Sentinel is one of the nine major kingdoms within Hammerfell and is the capital of both the Alik'r Desert region and the Myrkwasa region of the Alik'r (source: elderscrolls.fandom). With this knowledge, it's fair to assume Sentinel will have many desert locations.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. We still don't know exactly when The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel will be released, but we're now about seven years from its original announcement at E3 2018.

#4252. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4251. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4250. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

#4249. Japanese Charts: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Physical Takes The Lion's Share Of Its Japanese Sales

After Nintendo's reveal this week that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time had shifted 5.2 million units in its first four days, it will come as no surprise to hear that it's a smash hit in Japan. But still, Famitsu's latest numbers are in, and the physical is flying!

According to this week's chart, Link's latest produced ~537,000 physical sales in its chart debut — giving it the lion's share of Japan's 810,000 sales that Nintendo reported, and leaving around 273,000 sales for digital. As we say, it's hardly surprising, but still!

It makes all the other entries this week look piddly by comparison. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and Rhythm Heaven Groove round out the podium with a comparatively tiny 16,621 and 8,793 sales, respectively, and Stellar Blade: Complete Edition made its debut in fourth.

While Switch 2 sales are actually down following last week's bump, the console still leads this week's hardware chart by a comfortable margin. Nintendo's latest pulled in an additional ~53,000 sales this week, topping the PS5 Digital Edition, which came in with 11,377.

Once again, however, those Digital Edition sales swing things in Sony's favour over the Switch 1 when we look at the total SKU numbers for the week. The three PS5 systems combined this time for 11,699, while the Switch 1 units came in at 5,148.

#4248. The Sims 4 gets a bunch of free items inspired by Coach that you can use right now

As part of a free update, The Sims 4 has kicked off a new collaboration with Coach, which means there's free stuff for everyone.

The Sims 4’s first update of the year is here, though it may not be quite what you might have expected. The game’s latest patch mainly centres around a collaboration with Coach, the luxury fashion brand.

This obviously isn’t the game’s first collaboration with a known brand, though this one does include a lot of free items and accessories that anyone can make use of, even if they don’t care about Coach.

The Coach Collection brings nine new items to The Sims 4. They range from clothes and accessories you can use with Create a Sim, to decoration items available in Build Buy. There’s also The Carriage House, a new Gallery household where you can find three new roommates.

There’s a nice bit of variety in the options available, some casual and others more practical for your Sims to wear. Then there’s The Bag Room, which can also be grabbed from the Gallery. The room simply serves as a way for you to show off your Coach bags and trunks collection.

In case you missed it, The Sims’ development team recently shared an update on some of what we can expect in 2026, both for The Sims 4 as well as other projects currently in the works. It even included further confirmation, if any was needed, that Project Rene is a dedicated mobile off-shoot, and not — as many had long believed — The Sims 5.

The blog post also included a statement about EA’s imminent change of ownership, which many fear could alter the series’ inclusive and diverse nature, and the decisions made by its various teams.

#4247. The Best Rainbow Six Game is Getting an Unexpected Sequel

For nearly two decades, Rainbow Six: Vegas has been left in the past while Siege has become the face of the franchise. The two games offer very different experiences, though. Vegas was built around a proper campaign, room-clearing, and a squad that followed your orders. It's been a long time since Rainbow Six offered anything quite like it.

It was a huge disappointment when Ubisoft cancelled each of these games, and they deserve to be revisited at some point in the future.

Now, Insider Gaming reports that Ubisoft has greenlit a new Rainbow Six: Vegas project at Ubisoft Montreal. It's reportedly codenamed Spades, with a third entry considered more likely than a remake. Ubisoft hasn't announced anything yet, but a new Vegas campaign would be a welcome change of pace.

According to the report, Spades is one of three projects recently started at Ubisoft Montreal, including another game said to be linked to Rainbow Six. There's no word on what that other project might be. Spades itself is believed to be in early development, so its setting, features, platforms, and release window remain unknown.

The original Rainbow Six: Vegas arrived in 2006, followed by Vegas 2 in 2008. Both games streamlined some of the more demanding elements of the early Rainbow Six formula, but they didn't abandon squad tactics. Teammates could be ordered into position, stacked at doors, and sent in with different breach commands. The cover-based firefights could get hectic, but there was usually time to think about how to approach the next room.

The squad AI wasn't always up to the task, either. A badly timed move could turn a straightforward room-clearing attempt into a scramble to keep everyone alive. The teammates weren't terrible, but SWAT 4 generally did a better job with its AI officers. That's one area a sequel could improve without losing the appeal of the older games.

I used to watch Vegas gameplay on a TV show about video games as a kid. I only got around to playing both games years later, and they were well worth it.

I've played most of the Tom Clancy games  over the years, completing and even replaying almost all Ghost Recon and Splinter Cell titles multiple times. Vegas was more linear than some of them, but its mix of tactical gameplay and straightforward action worked particularly well.

The snake cam let you check behind a door before breaching, and different entry points kept encounters interesting. Cover was useful, but the squad commands were what made the firefights memorable. Vegas also placed second in our ranking of the best Tom Clancy games, behind Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory.

Siege has given Rainbow Six a strong multiplayer identity, but there's room for something different alongside it. The older games had campaigns and squad-focused missions that offered a change from competitive multiplayer. A new Vegas wouldn't need to follow the Siege formula. It could bring back a side of Rainbow Six that hasn't had much attention in years.

Siege has given Rainbow Six a strong multiplayer identity, but there's room for something different alongside it.

Rainbow Six Tactics is another welcome development. Turn-based strategy is a good fit for the squad-focused side of the series, and it doesn't need to resemble Vegas to be interesting. A new first-person campaign and a separate tactical strategy game could happily coexist.

As our coverage of Rainbow Six Tactics pointed out, Ubisoft is making it a fully single-player game without an in-game shop or microtransactions. It's currently scheduled for 2027, with Paul Bishop from Vegas 2 returning as the head of Rainbow. That connection is a nice touch, but the turn-based gameplay is interesting in its own right.

If Spades does turn out to be Vegas 3, it has a solid foundation to build on. Keep the squad commands, the room-clearing, and the single-player campaign; make the teammates a little smarter. There isn't much reason to turn it into something else.

The Division 2 is attempting to fuse its ongoing player bases via both Steam and Ubisoft Connect.

#4246. Holiday Gift Guide 2026

With the holiday gift-giving season upon us, it’s time to think about the gaming fans in your life and find the ideal present to brighten their day. And if you’re the gamer in the family, we always encourage you to circle relevant items in the coming pages and leave your magazine open in hard-to-miss locations around the house. We’ve scoured dozens of tech products, tabletop games, collectibles, and more to select and highlight some of the coolest items we found this year.

We recommended the Board shortly after its launch, but with its expanded game library and lower price than first-adopter rates, this holiday season is an ideal time to make the leap. This family-friendly platform features original games that sit comfortably between the digital and physical divide. The horizontally placed screen shows the backdrop of one of the several included games, or the sold-separately add-on games that have popped in since launch. Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. New subclasses, spells, creatures, magical items, and factions add thoughtful, intriguing options for both players looking to play someone new and DMs hunting for new story hooks and challenges. $50

If you’re as excited as we are about this month’s celebration of the Tomb Raider legacy (see p. 40), this centerpiece statue is an ideal fit for your collection. Standing roughly nine inches in height, Lara is poised for exploration in her original classic garb. The sculpt strikes a perfect balance between crisp detail and stylistic presentation, in line with that early version of the character; the metallic blue motorcycle paint is especially striking. $250

For players longing for the glory days of stand-up arcade games, it’s hard to beat Arcade 1Up’s approach. The team’s sturdy cabinets look and sound great as a marquee feature of your game room. The new Outrun machine features much of the original display art, a bright 19-inch screen, and responsive gas and brake pedals as you steer around those tight corners. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.
