#4245. Battlefield 6 Season 2 delayed like many of us expected, but we're getting a new update and a bonus battle pass path

Battlefield 6 has pushed back its next season by nearly a month in order to refine Season 2 content and implement more of players' feedback.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several new customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

#4244. Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.

#4243. Fable Quest Trailer Ratio’d And Compared To Dragon Age

Xbox has just released a new gameplay trailer for Fable showing one of the game’s quests, but it might not have been the best showcase since it’s being bombarded with dislikes.

Ever since the initial reveal trailer more than six years ago, Fable has easily been one of Xbox’s most highly anticipated games. That excitement has only increased with each gameplay showcase and trailer, which have shown just how far Playground Games has pushed the original trilogy’s mechanics, even if the reboot is leaving some things behind.

Of course, while most people are looking forward to Fable, it’s also been a target for online hate campaigns ever since the second trailer. Recent showings of Fable, including one that was focused on combat, have notably had a lot of backlash, and that drama has all come to a head with the latest trailer for the game.

Earlier this week, the official Fable YouTube account shared a new trailer for the game that highlights a quest where the Hero and Arden investigate what’s happening to Oakshire. The gameplay admittedly isn’t the most exciting thing in the world, since it mostly just shows the Hero walking through the area, getting in a fight, and talking to Arden before a big plot tease at the end.

Fable will let us hit on as many townsfolk as we want, but am I the only one who liked getting at least one proper romance option in Fable 3?

While it’s not a great showcase, the quest trailer is pretty harmless overall in my opinion and not that noteworthy. People don’t seem to agree with that, though, as the trailer is being ratio’d on YouTube with 4,200 dislikes compared to 3,400 likes as of the time of writing and an incredibly negative comments section with some brutal reactions.

One notable trend in the comments section is comparisons to Dragon Age: The Veilguard, with one popular comment calling it “Fable Age: The Veilguard”. Others are simply calling it out as a “disappointing” trailer that ended too soon and didn’t really show anything of substance. As one user puts it, “Is that really the best they can show?”

The Fable account is definitely seeing these negative comments too, as it’s heart-reacted the few positive ones praising the voice acting and graphics.

It’s not just the YouTube video that’s being slammed, either, as Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s post about the trailer on Twitter is also full of backlash and the usual “Sweet Baby Inc” comments over two female characters. Some of it is clearly bad faith, but I’d be very hard-pressed to say the footage was worthy of a trailer.

It's been a long, hard road back to success for Sports Interactive, but FM 27 is the game I hoped it would be and so much more.

#4241. Live Service Fatigue Claims One More Popular Shooter

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

Another ambitious online shooter is biting the dust, and this time, it seems that players won't even get the chance to return for one last update.

GFA Games has officially announced today that PIONER, its post-apocalyptic MMO inspired by titles like STALKER and Fallout, is shutting down. The studio is ending development, canceling future updates, and preparing to take the game's servers offline after failing to secure the funding necessary to keep the project running.

In an announcement shared on social media, the development team explained that maintaining PIONER required additional financial support, but they couldn’t find any. The studio had spent the past few months negotiating with existing and potential partners, hoping to find an investment deal that would allow development to continue and preserve the team.

Unfortunately, those discussions didn't lead anywhere. According to the developers, GFA Games no longer has enough money of its own to continue working on the game or maintain its server infrastructure.

After years of near radio silence, Fairgames has been canceled and its staff redistributed throughout Sony games.

“We were unable to agree on the funding needed to continue the project. The studio no longer has sufficient funds of its own to continue development and keep the servers running.”

Aleksandr Nikitin, CEO of GFA Games, even addressed the community, expressing his disappointment over the decision and apologizing to players who purchased PIONER expecting more updates. He explained that the team had envisioned a long future for the project and had been trying to find a way to keep both the game and its developers together.

The recent announcement effectively puts an end to those plans. Since PIONER is an online-only experience, shutting down its servers also means players will no longer be able to access the game once the infrastructure is taken offline.

It's quite an unfortunate outcome for a game that spent years building up expectations before finally arriving on Steam Early Access in December 2025. The post-apocalyptic MMO promised an enormous world filled with dangerous mutants, exploration, survival mechanics, and multiplayer activities, which initially attracted some attention on Steam, reaching a peak of more than 1,600 concurrent players around launch. However, that interest quickly faded. By September, its 24-hour peak had dropped to just 11 players, according to SteamDB.

GFA Games has officially announced today that PIONER, its post-apocalyptic MMO inspired by titles like STALKER and Fallout, is shutting down.

Unfortunately, its launch was plagued by technical issues, and these numbers show that the shooter struggled to maintain a consistent player base in the months that followed. Now, GFA Games revealed that it really was struggling to turn its project into a sustainable live-service experience.

Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble is being shuttered before it could even reach worldwide launch status.

It's always disappointing to see an ambitious multiplayer project disappear like this, especially when players have invested money and time into its world. But the studio thanked everyone who supported PIONER, reported bugs, created content, and helped build its community, while acknowledging that it couldn't deliver the future originally promised.

For now, the development team hasn't provided a specific date for when the servers will go offline. Still, with development and updates officially ending, PIONER's days are numbered. And while the game may not have reached the audience its developers hoped for, its shutdown is another reminder of how difficult it can be to keep an online-only game alive when the players and financial support aren't there.

#4240. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4239. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4237. Data Shows New Tactical Shooter Port Struck Gold With Console Plans

The surprise announcement of a Squad console port hit harder than a tank rolling through an undefended spawn point.

Taking the world’s most popular tactical shooter and moving to a platform that is typically associated with run-and-gun titles like Call of Duty and Overwatch was a bold move, but the numbers are finally in, and it looks like Offworld Industries played a blinder.

The battles on the Ottoman Front are about to get deadlier as Gallipoli targets hitreg issues.

The Squad console alpha test ran from October 16 to October 25, with a free experience limited exclusively to the PlayStation 5. During the nine days of testing, console players got to try a battle between the Ukrainian Armed Forces and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

Although Squad will have full crossplay between PC, PS5, and XBOX Series X/S, the test servers disabled it to give Sony’s faithful a smoother introduction to the game.

Today, OWI has finally published the data from the playtest, and the results are quite encouraging.

According to a social media post by the official Squad account today, just over 110 thousand PS5 players participated in the playtest.

That number in a vacuum doesn’t say much, but what’s impressive is that the Squad playtest led to over 50 thousand wishlists on PlayStation 5 alone, meaning a conversion rate of around 45%. Many an indie dev would caution that treating wishlists as guaranteed sales is a highway to heartbreak, and they’d be right, but at the present moment it’s still a showcase of the positive effect of the playtesting sessions.

The strong reception to the Squad PS5 alpha preview is also reflected in the player ratings. According to OWI, the game closed the testing sessions with a 4.5 out of 5 score. The PC version of Squad has an 83% positive rating on Steam and a 4.3 out of 5 score on the Epic Games Store, landing the console port slightly ahead of its peers, but ultimately in the same bracket.

Squad first came out in 2015, with humble beginnings as a crowdfunded spiritual successor to Battlefield 2’s Project Reality mod. The early versions of the game feel like a far cry from what we call Squad today, especially on the technical side.

According to producer Peter Maurice (full interview here), Squad is done “turning that corner where a lot of the major tech investment is done”, and that has allowed the team at Offworld Industries to turn its focus to new platforms and content.

Taking the world’s most popular tactical shooter and moving to a platform that is typically associated with run-and-gun titles like Call of Duty and Overwatch was a bold move

Currently, Squad runs on Unreal Engine 5.7. The transition from Unreal Engine 4 was “a massive challenge for a small studio,” but the performance benefits were felt on PC once the game found its footing.

According to Maurice, OWI has been planning a console port for as long as 3 years, but the project only transitioned from an idea into reality about a year ago, following the release of space bug shooter Starship Troopers Extermination. The studio was able to move developers who had worked on bringing this game to console and put them to work on Squad, making the transition a lot smoother.

The next big challenge for Squad’s console release will be building a community that can support itself. As Maurice explained to me, consoles do not have a “veterans that have been with us for years like on PC,” and that means players will need the game to help people learn even when a more experienced player is not around.

Squad is coming to PlayStation 5 and XBOX Series X/S sometime in 2027. Secret Mode’s Project Marketing Manager, Matthew Beckett, says a future playtest session is possible, but more info on that later.

#4236. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4232. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

#4230. Heartopia surprise launches on Steam and shockingly, everyone seems to be happy

Heartopia players didn't actually end up having to wait too long to play the game on Steam, which is certainly not what anyone expected.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

We’ve been playing a lot of Heartopia ourselves, and have been updating and expanding our guides. If you’re looking to get started, such as with how to add and play with friends, how to regain Energy, and how to unlock home plots, our guides offer the best place to start.

If you want to unlock Da Lucky Stikk, Ardcoat, and Codex Astartes, you need to first grab the Auspex on Desert Wasteland, which reveals the location of hidden items and marks them on the map across all 40K stages.

You can find the Auspex directly north of the spawn point—just keep heading in a straight line until you come across a chunky sci-fi remote.

Likewise, the Arcanoscope reveals secrets and marks them on the map across all Age of Sigmar stages, so it's necessary to find Kragg Blackhammer's Master Rune. You can find the Arcanoscope directly west from the spawn point on Gnarlwood.

PlayStation first-party developer Santa Monica Studio has delayed its upcoming action game, God of War Laufey, to May. More specifically, the PlayStation 5-exclusive title will now launch on May 20, representing a roughly three-month delay from the original February 16 release date.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," a statement from the studio reads. "We don't take for granted the trusted place in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey stars Faye, Kratos' deceased wife from his Norse adventures, after she ends up in the mysterious realm known as the Everywhen following her death. We'll have to wait a bit longer than expected now to see what her adventure entails.

#4227. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

The mailbox is looking per-ritty empty at the time of writing, and we'd wager it's down to a certain November game keeping you all occupied!

Knowing the original game like the back of my hand, I'm yet to walk into a room without going, "Oooh, look how they changed that bit!" But the one that has stood out to me the most so far is being able to ride Epona right up to the entrance to Kakariko Village without getting chucked off at the bottom of the stairs.

Does it change the game in any way at all? Absolutely not. But praise be to whichever innovative dev at Nintendo thought, 'What if Jim didn't have to sit through a backtracking animation every time he forgot to dismount quickly enough?'

The ragdoll may not be a substantial inclusion, but if I can pick between a stiff, canned animation of Link collapsing to the floor and seeing his lifeless body tumble into the rapids that lead up to Zora's Domain, you know what I'm going to choose.

The option to remove one of the few tweaks I haven’t enjoyed so far — Navi’s incessant dialogue boxes commenting on everything — is a godsend. I was concerned she’d spend the entire game puncturing the mood with “Oooh, big mountain!” and “Wow, great work!” and “OMG, that was a lucky escape!” (I’m paraphrasing, but that’s the gist), and she does.

Turning on the ‘Master’ display option, though, reduces the UI to the bare minimum, removing almost everything, including Navi’s dialogue boxes. So when I emerge onto Hyrule Field, the landscape speaks for itself (with a little help from the music). Bliss. Other people might enjoy her interjections, and yes, I will miss a cute line or two, but thanks for letting me turn off the running commentary, Nintendo.

Turning Grouch Mode off, the slingshot easter egg in the courtyard window is ace. And Kakariko feels more like a real place now. And those little rivulets on Hyrule Field add so much. And that part of Lon Lon... *babbling trails off...

Without heading into spoiler territory, I suppose my niche tweak (if it’s considered niche) would be the addition of Threads of Time, but more specifically the Tapestry.

I’ve filled out my tapestry now, but throughout each stage of Link’s journey it was nice to see the progress I was making. I jumped into the remake with the hope of experiencing it with fresh eyes (although I’d played the original), and it really felt like it at times. It was also a really good way for me to gauge what I could do next should I forget, collectables I likely still needed, or even secrets I still had to unlock.

It’s a very simple addition common in modern gaming, but a tweak which was needed.

I’m enjoying all the revamped music, but one arrangement that took me by surprise is when you encounter common or garden foes. There’s more urgency and danger now: notes are sharply cutting in, there’s a subtle, unnerving rise and fall in volume, and if the battle lasts long enough, it goes up a notch when a horn (I’m guessing!) is eventually layered on top.

For a track I hadn’t given a second’s thought to in the original, I’m now delighted every time an enemy nears.

Note. Very minor pre-Hyrule Field spoilers ahead...

Some of the subtle tweaks to Ocarina of Time’s narrative landed so well with me. I won’t go into the later examples, but I absolutely adored the moment when Link runs into both Mido and Saria after leaving the Deku Tree.

Mido, who feels much more fleshed out in the remake, expresses shock and immediate concern for the Deku Tree, while Saria is devastated at the thought of Link leaving Kokiri Forest. She leaves, heartbroken at Link’s decision, and it’s only when we exit the forest that she catches up to make amends and deliver the Fairy Ocarina.

This extra scene isn’t much in the grand scheme of things, but it really adds weight to Link’s departure, emphasising the home and friends that he’ll be leaving behind. I love it.

Jim came to Nintendo Life in 2022 and, despite his insistence that The Minish Cap is the best Zelda game and his unwavering love for the Star Wars prequels (yes, really), he has continued to write news and features on the site ever since.

Mask of Truth. don't even have to think about it. I love the flavour text.

Edit: I mean, it might not qualify as tiny neccessarily, but it is my favourite tweak. If I had to give an alternative, the Megaton Hammer given it can effectively replace bombs.

I enjoy the little tweaks they made to the quality of life of the dungeons:

1. No loading between rooms 2. Enemies don't respawn every time you re-enter a room 3. More visual differentiation between rooms, and indicators of 'where to go next'

Taken together, I felt like I spent a lot less time backtracking back and forth between identical-looking rooms and re-killing the same annoying enemies, it made the dungeons I've always found the most annoying in the original (Jabu Jabu, Water Temple, Beneath the Well, Shadow Temple) a lot more tolerable (the free camera and motion-control aiming helps a lot in this regard as well).

Ganon is far more challenging in this plus i like their connecting totk ganondorf malice with the final boss but over all i like everything about the game.

So far for me (still relatively early in the game) it's the additions of scenes like the one Ollie mentioned - anyway, great to hear about all these tweaks and looking forward to seeing what others will mention in the comments, too!

I love that the camera is fully usable in castle town. Makes it far more alive and more tragic when it's all destroyed.

They could've easily kept it faithful, but chose to expand it greatly.

Lil’ Link is just so stinkin’ cute, runnin’ around bein’ all cute and stuff

Also being able to actually control the camera is a big win for me ☑️

There's a lot of changes that avoid blindly guessing or taking chances, and previous secrets are re-implemented so you aren't reliant on things like the Stone of Agony (that required the rumble pak sold separately).

There's much less "how was I supposed to know?" moments. On one hand it's more accessible, on the other hand it's less cryptic and mysterious when you stumble into something, or learn from another source. These were always the smaller things that you didn't need to do to beat the game, anyway.

My favorite tweak is how they made Link leaving the cutscene where he gets the Fairy Ocarina more impactful.

In the original, he takes a couple tentative steps back, then leaves using his normal running animation. You could interpret it as emotional, but it could’ve also been just him walking away since it’s the normal movement animation.

I like that they emphasized that small detail by making it more obviously emotional in the way Link leaves. Just a small detail that reinterprets the original material in a way that I thought they might have been going for, but was unclear due to hardware limitations.

@bluemujika 70? Someone didn't get to buy it from Walmart or Amazon for 60

Cutscenes in general are much improved while keeping the tone of the original. Link getting knocked TF out by Darunia had me in stitches. Ruto (especially in Japanese had the Ojousama mannerisms dialed up while somehow making her sound …less spoiled?), just Ruto. Anytime they lean on Zelda being a badarse is always a plus in my book and woo she’s even cooler y’all while still having an air of vulnerability and gravitas. They over did her guilt a bit though. Loved Impa as usual and Nabooru felt more like a warrior for justice this time around (she has never liked Ganondorf, but she really felt he didn’t deserve blind praise simply because he was their king due to a genetic quirk). They made Mido somewhat decent. I am anti bully and feel those types of people don't change, but I sorta felt bad for Mido.

I have never hated Navi, but I teared up when she left at the end. I really enjoyed hanging out with that little lightbulb. When you meet a great fairy her comment on the fountain made me laugh. You could almost hear her trying to figure out to become a great fairy. I do miss her hanging out in Link’s hat though.

I’ll admit muscle memory makes me not try a lot of stuff so I tend to notice scene changes, but I agree with bringing Epona to the gate. My eyebrows went up at that. Grottos are way easier to find (thank you!). I don’t like that redeads run at you now. F that. Somehow Dark Link feels like more of an ahole?

Morpha boss fight was fun this time. (As was Ganon). And the shadow and camera angle was good for my visually impaired self. I was concerned. I spend too much time reflecting back beamos lasers.

Also whomever designed new dead hand? Yeah I wanna cuss that person out.

My favorite though? THE ZORA ARE FREE (and all have the flu but still…)!!

How that stupid Owl doesnt ask if you understand, ITS THE BEST!!

Oh definitely the little tassels on Ganondorf's armour.

If I'm being serious, I liked that new item that allowed you to summon a business scrub at will. Didn't think I'd actually use them but they came in handy in a pinch.

The extra bits of context in the cutscenes are great. The story just makes more sense with them.

Just finished a 100% play through today and I have to say i'm mighty impressed.

I went back to play the original for the first time after beating the remake. Besides the obvious improvements like camera controls, being able to save and quit and be in the same area is game-changing. The first time I saved in the original was in Kakariko and when I opened the game to be back in Link's house, I was pretty peeved...

Also after dying to the big octorock and having to run back to the boss room every time with only 3 hearts, that was pretty annoying but I'm not sure if it works like that in the remake considering how few times I died. OoT64 is definitely harder, but i think it comes from the single stick control more than actual difficulty changes in the remake

Also one little note, I did see a lot of bad-faith haters complaining about the changed dialogue, but I have honestly enjoyed the original writing and lack of shoddy voice acting in the original more than the remake so far. It does kinda feel like they watered it down for the remake, and the voice acting does not help that at all... even if the cutscenes are pretty

@solarwolf07 Yeah, it's kind of funny how a lot of the difficulty change feels like it's mostly just due to the controls and camera being so much easier so you're not constantly getting merced by flaming bats you can't get the camera to focus on or whatever. It feels like you actually get fewer hearts and fairies and stuff in dungeons so I don't think it's like the game constantly giving you health that it didn't previously (aside from the fairy thoughts, if you get those).

The fact that you can wear masks as an adult! I actually specifically asked for this in a thread a couple weeks ago. Now I don't have to go back to child form every time I come across a new gossip stone just to find out what it says. And of course I can read everyone's thoughts in the future to find out how they have changed.

The emotional beats between link and saria are tweaked just enough, that my god. It just hits you like a bus. Even when you just talk to her at her spot outside the forest temple, that sense of leaving childhood is so intense in a way I did not expect

Probably thawing Zora's Domain. Nothing of substance to do there afterward which is why I'd consider it tiny but it was a big loose end to leave in the original and it's nice having the quick access tunnel from Lake Hylia working as an adult.

The movement, this is the best any character has controlled in possibly any game I've ever played. I was very worried that they were going to introduce momentum based movement like how characters control in more realistic AAA games (Uncharted for example seems to be the template for this and many other games in the same vain). But Link has a bit of that at the start of his run but they kept it very arcade like where any direction he goes is almost instant, combine that with being able to walk over any terrain and perform jumps and acrobatics in the environment and you're left with a result that enhances the greatest game of all time to an even higher level. The longer I played the game the more impressed I became with how intuitive it was to control Link and cannot praise the work the developers did enough.

For me it's Navi extra dialogue, sorry to disagree Gavin. But her having extra flavortext makes her feel more like a character than a tool to explain and target enemies. And now that she feels more like an individual the game feels like your playing it with a buddy! I even used her more not for actual help but because i was curious as to what she had to say.

I like that the Mask of Truth can actually be used to read minds now! It's not just backstory flavour, it functions like that for the player too.

@Ryu_Niiyama I really like how all the Zora caught a cold because they have been frozen 😄

@EarthboundBenjy Also just the fact that it can be worn as adult Link. You encounter and can speak to so many more of the gossip stones through just playing the game instead of having to back track as a child.

I like that the Gerudo's are a little more aggressive and mindful of their surroundings now. It made finding the carpenters more challenging!

The Cuccos thing is slightly harder as you now have to remember to jump. Along with loads of other bits being harder if your a dum dum and forget to jump. Some changes like the volley bit and the 2nd dungeon boss as child link are easier. And most of the time when you forget to jump and get punished your not even that annoyed about it and enjoy the challenge of remember to jump lol.

Haven't played a whole lot yet, but the lack of loading screens between buildings and most areas is pretty cool, and something I was hoping for. Being able to see into Lon Lon Ranch from Hyrule Field and then walk right in is pretty damn cool.

I like when you find Richard, the fat lady lets you ride her around Hyrule Town to say thanks

All replaying it has done for me is to wish there’s a new Zelda made in the same format. An “ocarina 2” if you like.

I love BotW and ToTK but damn this old setup is a joy to play. The old dungeons, creativity everywhere. It’s nice not having a stamina bar and a condensed world for a change. This to me really FEELS like a Zelda, much more than the new open world games do.

I'm only at Goron City (really taking my time to absorb everything) but so far, it's definitely the music. I don't know if that qualifies as a tiny tweak, but it truly makes the game even more special. I can't get enough.

There’s chanting in the music for the fire temple again. Albeit somewhat different than the original score

Poor Navi. She just can't catch a break, even if her interjections are just little speech bubbles now. Eternally cursed. lol

My number one favorite change is the orchestral score. It really goes hard, even when pushing/pulling the master sword. But yeah Nintendo knocked it out of the universe with this. WOW.

Lmao… for a moment I read “who’s your favorite tiny twink?” … and I was da fck?

Also… the most important one that couldn’t be done in the original. The Zora are free at last!

@ChromaticDracula The orchestral versions of the music are OUTSTANDING! I'm always curious how nobody seems to mention this...

My favourite minor tweak is that the hookshot can hit those eye switches now. That means you can legitimately do water temple first if you want. Good change.

My least favourite tweak is how they've streamlined dungeons by taking out locks and keys. They don't feel as difficult or labyrinthian now.

@Aurumonado I always did water temple first ...Gotta rescue the wife before the friend!

@DanElectrode very true. On the topic of heart drops, I noticed that heart drops in the original seem to spawn three instead of one, which pleasantly surprised me haha

I’m not going to go into specifics and spoil anything, but for me it’s post-Water Temple Zora Domain.

I just love the ability to jump. Feels like some Mario game sometimes because I jump like an idiot everywhere 🤣 Especially from rock to rock, really funny to do !

I did not play much of the original, so I can't compare extensively, but one aspect I really like too is the fact you can explore cities at night now ! Kokiri forest is so beautiful at this time of day !

Putting Din's Fire in the Death Mountain GFF rather than the hidden Hyrule Castle one.

Breath of the wild references love.But a fairy now only heals 6 hearts not full health hate.

Difficult to remember because I only played Zelda Ocarina once back in the day, and revisiting it in recent years I was confronted with a blurring, clunky mess and barely lasted an hour in it. The remake is a godsend for someone like me eager to experience it again without suffering the many archaic elements that present themselves today.

I mostly notice that everything feels nicer. There's none of the clunkiness whether that be in the controls, obviously a vastly improved frame rate, and general design tweaks. One that I did note is the narrow path in the Fire Temple where a fall meant a long walk all the way back to trying it again. Boring! Now, Link will cling to the ledge and recover, or will fall into a lava pit, lose health, and respawn.

I bet this is one of the petty examples that IGN used to say this version of Ocarina is "easier" in its obvious agenda to not score it a 10. Whereas to sane people, the punishment from that fall is purely cheap game design. The path is easy to traverse as long as it's not rushed, so clinging to the ledge or losing health is an excellent two-stage warning to be careful compared to the previous brutal method after some simple carelessness. That is much more in sync with the ethos of Ocarina whereas in something like Ghosts N Goblins, that sort of cheap punishment is to be expected!

There are a lot of little things I like. Pro / Master HUD is great. Jumping changes gameplay. The cutscenes are astonishing, especially the scene you get the master sword for the first time. The environment changes with the modern rendering makes everything feel more natural and true to their vision. And as others mentioned, the orchestral music is just beautiful.

All great but the best? It’s the three C’s. Character, Camera, and Controls for me.

We take it for granted but dual sticks and 100% camera control makes such a fundamental difference in the gameplay that I truly believe it will surprise many how it feels to go back to play the original. It just gives me even more freedom. Ocarina of Time was the first game I played on N64. It was my first 3D game and introduced me to “open worlds”. To now experience that with modern camera controls with all the other changes just really seals the deal for me. Link does what I want, when I want it, and how I want. I never feel cheated. I feel like when I run up and jump near Epona, it just works and Link mounts correctly. I like when I walk around with my shield up, he keeps walking forward but I can pivot my shield to the left or right. I can control my sword swing direction. I can swing the camera just where I need it and it doesn’t clip into the environment. They way Link responds to all my inputs just feels… right.

A lot of people will go back to the original. It was will still hold up very well, but all things considered, the camera controls makes the biggest difference to me. I can say so far, this is my favourite version of Ocarina of Time and I am surprised I feel this way. This game beat my expectations.

If I had any minor criticisms about the controls, it’s simply the fact I can’t be as hardcore as in the N64 version, and I don’t have a separate dedicated button to raise my shield while Z-targeting like in the original version.

They nailed the feeling of walking on ice! The frosting and the snow in the Ice Cavern is amazing. Actually made me reach for a blanket!

#4225. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.
